answers.question: Does the circuit in the figure fail to oscillate if CL becomes arbitrarily large?

answer.text:
Yes—**for finite-gain inverters, a sufficiently large \(C_L\) eventually quenches oscillation.**

Let the loaded node have pole \(p_1\), and the other two nodes have poles \(p_2,p_3\). Three inversions already give \(180^\circ\), so the poles must add another \(180^\circ\):

\[
\tan^{-1}\frac{\omega_0}{p_1}+
\tan^{-1}\frac{\omega_0}{p_2}+
\tan^{-1}\frac{\omega_0}{p_3}=180^\circ .
\]

As \(C_L\to\infty\), \(p_1\to0\). The phase condition then forces \(\omega_0\) to a finite value set by the other poles, e.g. \(\omega_0\approx\sqrt{p_2p_3}\). But the gain of the loaded stage at that frequency is roughly

\[
|M_1|\approx \frac{A_1 p_1}{\omega_0}
= \frac{g_{m1}}{\omega_0 C_L}\to 0 .
\]

So the **phase** condition can still be approached, but the **loop-gain** condition fails. For identical other stages, the limit is roughly when

\[
\frac{C_L}{C_0} \gtrsim \frac{A_0^3}{2},
\]

where \(A_0\) is the inverter low-frequency gain and \(C_0\) the other node capacitance.

Caveat: in an ideal “logic delay” model, any finite \(C_L\) just lowers the frequency and \(f_{\rm osc}\to0\) as \(C_L\to\infty\). The gain-collapse argument is the finite-gain/RC oscillator criterion.

answer.text:

\[
L(s)=-\frac{A_v^{3}}{(1+s/\omega_1)(1+s/\omega_0)^2 } .
\]

Oscillation needs \(|L|=1\) at the frequency where the three poles add \(180^\circ\) of lag. Because \(\omega_1\ll\omega_0\), the loaded stage contributes essentially its full \(90^\circ\) long before the others, so the remaining \(90^\circ\) must come from the two fast stages — i.e. each supplies \(45^\circ\), forcing the frequency to \(\omega\approx\omega_0\). There,

\[
|L|\;\approx\;\underbrace{\frac{A_v}{k}}_{\text{loaded stage}}
\underbrace{\frac{A_v}{\sqrt2}\frac{A_v}{\sqrt2}}_{\text{two fast stages}}
=\frac{A_v^{3}}{2k}.
\]

Requiring \(|L|\ge 1\) gives

\[
k \;\lesssim\; \frac{A_v^{3}}{2}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
C_L \;\lesssim\; \frac{A_v^{3}}{2}\,C_{\text{node}} .
\]

(Equivalently, the Routh–Hurwitz condition on  
\((1+s/\omega_1)(1+s/\omega_0)^2+A_v^3=0\) fails when \(\omega_1/\omega_0\) drops below roughly \(2/A_v^3\); the right‑half‑plane pair collapses onto the real axis and all poles move into the left half plane.)

Intuitively: once \(C_L\) makes that node vastly slower than the other two, the two fast inverters respond “instantly,” so their two inversions cancel. The loaded inverter then just sees its own output fed back to its input — an inverter biased at its trip point with an integrating capacitor — which is a stable, non‑oscillatory negative‑feedback loop. So as \(C_L\to\infty\) the ring does not merely slow down without bound; past \(C_L\sim A_v^3 C_{\text{node}}/2\) it stops oscillating and settles at the trip point.

\[
|A_v|^3 \ge \frac{2(q+1)^2}{q},
\]

so for large \(q\),

\[

\]

answers.question: If we double the widths of the NMOS and PMOS devices in the figure, what happens to the phase noise?

answer.text:
The phase‑noise power spectral density drops by a factor of two — i.e. \(\mathcal{L}\{\Delta f\}\) improves by about **3 dB** — at essentially the **same oscillation frequency**.

Why: with \(L\) and \(V_{DD}\) fixed, doubling every \(W\) doubles each device’s \(g_m\) and drive current, but it also doubles the load capacitance that each inverter must drive (the next stage’s gate cap plus its own drain cap). Since \(I\propto W\) and \(C\propto W\), the stage delay \(\tau\sim C V_{DD}/I\) is unchanged, so \(f_0\) stays put. The voltage swing remains roughly rail‑to‑rail, so the maximum charge swing \(q_{\max}=C V_{DD}\) doubles (\(q_{\max}^2\times4\)), while each transistor’s thermal noise current \( \overline{i_n^2}=4kT\gamma g_m\) only doubles. Hence

\[
S_\phi \propto \frac{\Gamma_{\rm rms}^2\,\overline{i_n^2}}{q_{\max}^2\,\Delta\omega^2}
\;\propto\;\frac{W}{W^2}=\frac1W ,
\]

so \(S_\phi\) halves (\(-3\) dB). (The same \(1/W\) scaling holds for the up‑converted flicker part, so the \(1/f^3\) corner stays roughly in place and the whole spectrum just shifts down ~3 dB.)

Cost: power dissipation and area roughly double. Equivalently, this is just the usual ring‑oscillator trade‑off \(\mathcal{L}\propto 1/P\) at fixed \(f_0\) and offset, so the oscillator **figure of merit is unchanged** — you bought 3 dB of phase noise with 3 dB more power. Caveat: this assumes device capacitance dominates the node; a large fixed wiring/load capacitance would break the scaling and also move \(f_0\).

- The circuit linearized about the oscillation is **linear periodically time-varying**, not a simple linear time-invariant resistor.

Thus there is no unique scalar \(R_X\) unless the measurement is defined more precisely. For a slow supply perturbation, an appropriate effective resistance is

\[

=
\frac{d}{dV_{DD}}
\left[
\frac{1}{T_0}
\int_0^{T_0} i_{DD}(t)\,dt
\right],
\]

where both the current waveform and \(T_0\) may depend on \(V_{DD}\). For a small AC perturbation while oscillating, a periodic-AC or harmonic-balance analysis gives a frequency-dependent admittance and possibly sidebands.

=
\left[
\frac{d\langle I_{DD}(t)\rangle}{dV_{DD}}
\right]^{-1},
\]

\[

\approx
\left[

\right]^{-1}.

answers.question: Analyze the arrangement in the figure.

answer.text:
**What it is.** The drawing is a closed feedback loop containing two complementary clocked switches (transmission‑gate style) and three inverters: **Inv₁** in the “sample” branch and a series inverter pair after the CK̄ switch. Because CK and CK̄ are never both 1, one switch is always open, so the loop is never continuously closed. It is therefore **not a free‑running ring oscillator** but a two‑phase (complementary‑clock) dynamic master–slave stage whose output is fed back to its input.

Let **Q** be the fed‑back node (left end = right end of the bottom rail), **X** the input of Inv₁, **B = Inv₁ output = ¬X**, and **C** the input of the inverter pair. Since two inverters cancel, the pair gives **Q = C** (with gate delay).

| Clock phase | Switch CK | Switch CK̄ | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| CK = 1 (CK̄ = 0) | closed | open | Master samples: X = Q, so B = ¬Q. Slave is open, so C (and hence Q) is held dynamically. Output does **not** change. |
| CK ↓ (1→0) | opens | closes | Master freezes at B = ¬Q; slave passes it: C ← B, so **Q ← ¬Q**. |
| CK = 0 | open | closed | X is isolated (holds old Q); B is frozen, so Q stays at ¬Q. Next CK ↑ only re‑samples the new Q. |

**Next‑state equation.**
\[
Q^{+}=\overline{Q}\quad\text{updated on the falling edge of CK}
\]
(equivalently on the rising edge of CK̄). Thus the arrangement is a **toggle flip‑flop with T = 1**, i.e. a **divide‑by‑two frequency divider**: \(f_{out}=f_{CK}/2\). It is functionally a D flip‑flop with **D = Q̄**; Inv₁ provides the Q̄ and the inverter pair acts as the slave/storage buffer.

**Design constraints / caveats**
- CK and CK̄ must be complementary and **non‑overlapping**. If both switches conduct together, the three inverters (odd count = 3) close around the loop and the circuit becomes a 3‑stage ring oscillator / races instead of toggling.
- When a switch is open, the corresponding node (X or C) is held only by **dynamic charge** on its capacitance, so there is a **minimum usable clock frequency** (leakage limits hold time). The **maximum frequency** is set by the sum of the switch + inverter delays around the half‑loop.
- A small “both‑off” gap is harmless (dynamic hold); an overlap (both‑on) is the dangerous condition.

answers.question: Analyze the arrangement in the figure.

answer.text:
**What it is:** a two‑phase (complementary‑clock) dynamic toggle stage — i.e. a master–slave **T flip‑flop with T = 1**, which works as a **÷2 frequency divider** (one ripple‑counter bit). It is *not* a free‑running ring oscillator, even though three inverting stages appear in the loop.

Label the nets: **a** = feedback return (same net as the final output **f**), **b** = input of Inv₁ (after the CK switch), **c** = output of Inv₁, **d** = input of the 2nd inverter (after the CK̄ switch), **e**, then **f**.

| Phase | CK switch | CK̄ switch | What happens |
|---|---|---|---|
| φ₁: CK = 1 | closed | open | **b ← a = f.** The pair Inv₂+Inv₃ (two inversions = buffer) passes the charge stored on **d**, so **f = d**. Inv₁ drives **c = b̄**, but it is blocked by the open CK̄ switch. Node **d** is held dynamically. |
| φ₂: CK = 0 | open | closed | **b** is held dynamically (= previous f). **d ← c = Inv₁(b) = b̄**, then **f = d** through the two inverters. |

Tracking the held value **s** of node **d** from one cycle to the next gives

\[
s_{n+1}=\overline{s_n}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad f_{n+1}=\overline{f_n},
\]

so the output toggles once per clock period: **f_out = f_CK / 2**. The output **f** changes on the **falling edge of CK** (when the CK̄ switch closes) and is then stable for a full clock period; node **b** is the complementary “master” copy that updates on the rising edge.

Key points / caveats

- **Why it doesn’t oscillate:** a permanently closed 3‑inverter loop is a ring oscillator (odd inversion). Here the complementary switches guarantee that in every half‑cycle one switch is open, so the regenerative loop is broken and the transfer is always master→slave with exactly **one** net inversion per full period (Inv₁ inverts b→d; Inv₂+Inv₃ make d→b non‑inverting).
- **Dynamic storage:** during the off‑phase the state lives only on parasitic capacitance (node **d** in φ₁, node **b** in φ₂). Hence there is a **minimum clock frequency** (leakage) and the circuit is sensitive to **charge sharing** and **clock feedthrough**. The switches should be full transmission gates (nMOS∥pMOS).
- **Non‑overlap required:** CK and CK̄ must be break‑before‑make. If both switches conduct simultaneously, all three inverters are in a closed odd loop → transient oscillation/contention and possible crowbar current.
- **Speed limits:** max f_CK is set by the switch + inverter delays (the transferred level must settle within a half‑period); min f_CK is set by leakage of the floating nodes.

Use: cascaded (CK of the next stage = f of this one) it forms the LSB of an asynchronous ripple counter, with the usual dynamic‑logic precautions.

answers.question: How does the red inverter in the figure affect the performance?

answer.text:
It hurts the circuit — it does not act as a harmless “extra” inverter.

Electrically the red gate is wired from the returned output node (the far‑left node that comes back along the bottom wire, call it **L**) to the internal node between Inv₁ and the CK̄ switch (call it **N**). So it sits in parallel with the “CK switch + Inv₁” path and bypasses the CK‑controlled isolation.

Consequences:

- When CK is high (CK switch on, CK̄ switch off) it merely reinforces Inv₁ (both drive N = ¬L), so it only adds load capacitance on L and N.
- When CK goes low (CK switch opens, CK̄ switch closes) the master node at the input of Inv₁ is left holding the old value, while L has been updated by the right‑hand pair. The red inverter then drives N from the *new* L while Inv₁ still drives N from the *old* stored value → the two inverters fight (short‑circuit/crowbar current).
- Worse, with the CK̄ switch closed the path L → red inverter → N → CK̄ switch → two output inverters → bottom wire back to L contains an **odd number of inversions**. That turns the slave half‑cycle into an astable/ring loop instead of a clean latch, so the output can glitch or oscillate rather than toggle once per clock.

Net effect on performance: degraded noise margin and setup/hold behavior, possible logic failure of the divide‑by‑2/toggle action, plus extra dynamic and contention power and added capacitive loading — i.e., slower and less reliable. A proper keeper for the floating node would feed back around Inv₁ (from N to the input of Inv₁), not from the returned output forward to N.

answers.question: How does the red inverter in the figure affect the performance?

answer.text:
The red device is an **ungated inverter wired in parallel with the clocked first stage**: its input sits on the left‑hand/return node (the CK side) and its output sits on the output node of **Inv₁** (before the CK̄ switch). Because it has no series clock switch, it couples those two nodes in **both** clock phases.

Performance consequences:

- **It breaks the high‑impedance hold phase.** When CK is low the black path through Inv₁ is supposed to be cut off, but the red inverter still drives Inv₁’s output node from the return line. That node then fights the right‑hand inverter pair, giving **driver contention / static short‑circuit current** and a loss of noise margin (the stage no longer truly holds a dynamic value).
- **Loop parity is changed.** Around the right‑hand feedback path (through the CK̄ switch and the last two inverters) the red inverter adds one more inversion, i.e. the closed loop contains an **odd** number of inversions. Thus, instead of a stable/regenerative hold, the loop tends to **race or oscillate**, and the extra gate delay shifts the oscillation period/duty cycle.
- **Drive vs. load trade‑off.** In the active (CK) phase it is in parallel with Inv₁, so it lowers the effective output resistance and pulls the intermediate node faster, but it also adds input capacitance to the return/CK node and output capacitance to Inv₁’s output. Net: more drive on one node, more load on the previous/feedback node.
- **Power goes up** from both the extra CV²f switching and the contention (crowbar) current during the CK̄ interval.

In short: unless it is deliberately made very weak (a “keeper”), the red inverter mainly **degrades hold robustness and increases power**, while only modestly speeding the active edge; functionally it turns what would be an even (latching) feedback into an odd (switching/oscillating) one.

Most importantly, it misses that the unclocked loop can overwhelm the main path at low clock rates, raising the minimum usable frequency, and instead frames the effect mainly as generic hold degradation and power increase.

answers.question: How does the red inverter in the figure affect the performance?

answer.text:
The red device is wired from the left‑hand (CK/input) node directly to the output node of **Inv₁**, i.e. in parallel with the clocked branch “CK‑switch + Inv₁,” and it is **not itself gated by the clock**. That changes the latch in a few important ways:

* **It removes the high‑impedance (purely dynamic) interval.** When the CK switch is off, the node after Inv₁ would otherwise be left floating on capacitance. The red inverter keeps driving that node, so the level is restored/held against leakage and coupling. Result: better noise margin, full logic swing, and no lower limit on clock frequency (no refresh requirement) — essentially a “staticized”/keeper action.

* **Faster, sharper transition in the transparent phase.** While the CK switch is on, the internal node is driven by both Inv₁ and the red inverter, so the effective drive resistance is lower and the edge is less sensitive to the switch on‑resistance and to clock slew.

* **But it must be ratioed (made weak).** Because it is always on, whenever the feedback/storage path wants the opposite value, the write driver has to **overpower** the red inverter. If it is sized like a normal inverter, you get large contention/short‑circuit current, higher dynamic power, slower overwriting, and in the limit the latch may fail to change state. So it is typically built weak (small W/L, long channel or high |Vₜ|) — strong enough to hold against leakage, weak enough to lose during a write.

* **Extra loading and clock‑power.** It adds gate capacitance to the left/CK node and diffusion capacitance to the internal node, raising clock‑distribution power and slightly loading the preceding stage.

* **Timing/skew impact.** Together with the CK and CK̄ switches, its delay contributes to the local CK→CK̄ non‑overlap. Too little non‑overlap gives a brief both‑switches‑on window (race‑through/crowbar current); too much leaves the node momentarily dynamic. Thus it also helps set the minimum usable clock pulse width and the setup/hold behavior.

In short: it trades a little power, area and contention (and a sizing constraint) for a static, better‑driven internal node — improved robustness and edge quality, provided the inverter is kept weak enough to be overpowered during a write.

But it miscasts the path as a keeper and claims it removes the low-frequency limit; in fact, the unclocked branch can overwhelm the main path at low clock rates, raising the minimum usable frequency.

answers.question: How do we optimize the circuit shown in the figure for the NF if Rin must remain equal to 50 Ohm?

answer.text:
Treat \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) as one transconductor: because both gates are driven and both drains are tied together,

\[
g_m=g_{m1}+g_{m2},\qquad r_o=r_{o1}\!\parallel r_{o2},
\]

with shunt–shunt feedback through \(R_F\). Let the source resistance be \(R_s=50\ \Omega\) (\(G_s=1/R_s\), \(G_F=1/R_F\)) and take \(C_1\) as a short at the operating frequency (it only blocks DC; the gate is self‑biased through \(R_F\)).

**Input match constraint.** A nodal analysis gives the real low/mid‑band input resistance

\[
\boxed{\;R_{\rm in}=\frac{R_F+r_o}{1+g_m r_o}=R_s\;}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
R_F=R_s+r_o\,(g_mR_s-1),
\]

so you need \(g_mR_s>1\) (otherwise the forward \(g_m\) cancels the feed‑through, \(A_v\!=\!1-R_F/R_s\to0\), and the noise factor blows up). Note the important point: the feedback lets \(g_m\) exceed \(1/R_s\) while still giving \(R_{\rm in}=50\ \Omega\) — unlike a common‑gate stage, the noise match is (partly) decoupled from the power match.

**Noise factor.** Including only channel thermal noise  
(\(\overline{i_{n}^{2}}=4kT(\gamma_1 g_{m1}+\gamma_2 g_{m2})\equiv4kT\,\gamma_{\rm eff}g_m\)) and the \(R_F\) noise,

\[
F-1=
\frac{(G_s+G_F)^2\,\gamma_{\rm eff}g_m+(G_s+g_m)^2G_F}
{(g_m-G_F)^2\,G_s}.
\]

Imposing the match equation and defining \(m=g_mR_s\) and the intrinsic gain \(A_0=g_mr_o\gg1\), this reduces to approximately

\[
\boxed{\;F\;\approx\;1+\underbrace{\frac{\gamma_{\rm eff}}{g_mR_s}}_{\text{channel}}
+\underbrace{\frac{(m+1)^2}{m(m-1)}\frac{1}{A_0}}_{R_F\text{ noise}}\;}
\qquad (m>1).
\]

So both excess‑noise terms are driven down by **large \(g_mR_s\)** and by **large intrinsic gain \(g_mr_o\)**, while \(m\to1\) must be avoided.

**How to optimize, given \(R_{\rm in}=50\ \Omega\) is fixed**

1. **Exploit the current reuse.** \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) share the same bias current and their \(g_m\)’s add. Size them (self‑biased through \(R_F\) near \(V_{DD}/2\)) so that \(g_{m1}\approx g_{m2}\), i.e. roughly \((W/L)_2/(W/L)_1\approx\mu_n/\mu_p\). For a given supply current this nearly doubles \(g_m\) versus a single device, halving the \(\gamma_{\rm eff}/(g_mR_s)\) term (or halving the current for the same NF).

2. **Maximize \(g_m/I_D\) and \(A_0=g_mr_o\).** Bias at low overdrive (moderate inversion) and use a channel length that keeps \(\lambda\) small; this raises \(g_m\), \(r_o\) and hence \(A_0\), reducing the channel term and suppressing the feedback‑resistor term. Then set \(R_F\) from the match equation above (for high gain \(R_F\approx R_s(1+A_0)\)).

3. **Keep \(m=g_mR_s\) comfortably \(>1\).** Do not choose \(R_F\) so small that \(g_m\approx G_F\); there the signal gain vanishes and \(F\) diverges.

4. **Add the gate parasitics at RF.** The real optimum is finite because the input is not inductively tuned: minimize gate resistance with many short fingers (\(F\) gains \(\approx R_g/R_s\)) and include induced gate noise, which grows like \(\omega^2C_{gs}^2/(g_m)\,R_s\). Balancing \(\gamma_{\rm eff}/(g_mR_s)\) (falls with \(W\) and \(I_D\)) against \(R_g/R_s\) and the induced‑gate term gives the optimum device width/bias; \(C_1\) is simply made large enough to be a short at \(f_0\).

In short: with the \(50\ \Omega\) match enforced by \(R_F\), you cannot “noise‑match” independently; you minimize NF by getting the largest possible \(g_m\) and \(g_mr_o\) per unit current (the complementary pair is chosen exactly for that), then setting \(R_F\) from the match equation and minimizing gate resistance/induced gate noise.

At the operating frequency, treat \(C_1\) as a short and neglect gate current for the real part. Define

\[
g_m=g_{m1}+g_{m2},\qquad g_o=g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}+g_L,\qquad G_F=\frac1{R_F}.
\]

Then

\[
A_v=\frac{v_o}{v_i}
= -\frac{g_m-G_F}{g_o+G_F},
\qquad
Y_{in}=G_F(1-A_v)=\frac{g_m+g_o}{1+g_oR_F}.
\]

The constraint \(\Re\{Y_{in}\}=1/50\,\Omega\) gives, with \(A=|A_v|\),

\[
\boxed{R_F = 50(1+A)}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{g_m=\frac1{50}+A g_o } .
\]

So \(R_F\) is **not** an independent noise-optimization resistor; it is fixed after the gain/output conductance are chosen.

For noise, the low-frequency matched result is approximately

\[
F \approx 1+
\frac{\gamma_{\rm eff}}{g_m 50}
+\frac{50}{R_F}
\qquad (g_m 50 \gg 1),
\]

with

\[
\gamma_{\rm eff}=\frac{\gamma_1 g_{m1}+\gamma_2 g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}
\]

(use \(\gamma/\alpha\) if your noise model is defined with \(g_{d0}\)). More exactly, with \(x=g_m50\), \(\lambda=g_o50\), and \(A=(x-1)/\lambda\),

\[
F=1+
\frac{\gamma_{\rm eff}x(A+2)^2+(A+1)(x+1)^2}
{A^2(x+\lambda)^2}.
\]

Therefore the NF-optimization direction is:

- make \(g_m50\) comfortably larger than 1; the region \(g_m \approx 1/R_F\) is bad because feedforward through \(R_F\) cancels the transistor current and the gain collapses;
- for a fixed bias current, maximize \(g_m/I_D\): low overdrive, both devices in saturation, current-reuse NMOS+PMOS pair;
- maximize output resistance/loop gain so that, for the same 50 Ω input, \(A\) and hence \(R_F\) are large; this reduces the feedback-resistor noise term;
- size \(M_1/M_2\) for low \(\gamma_{\rm eff}\) and low parasitics. If \(\gamma_n\approx\gamma_p\), the exact N/P ratio mainly sets DC balance/headroom; often \(W_p/W_n\approx \mu_n/\mu_p\) for symmetric swing;
- use many fingers/short gate interconnects to minimize gate resistance, make \(C_1\) large and high-Q, and tune out the input capacitance with a lossless reactance. Any loss before the gates adds essentially dB-for-dB to NF.

After every sizing/bias change, recompute \(R_F\) from the boxed match equation so that \(R_{in}\) returns to 50 Ω, then verify NF, stability, gain, bandwidth and linearity with the PDK noise model.

A_v=\frac{v_o}{v_i}=\frac{1-g_mR_F}{1+R_F/r_o}=-a .
\]

The low-frequency input resistance is

\[
R_{in}=\frac{R_F+r_o}{1+g_m r_o}.
\]

Imposing \(R_{in}=R_S=50\ \Omega\) gives

\[
\boxed{R_F=R_S+r_o\left(g_mR_S-1\right)}
\]

or equivalently

\[
\boxed{R_F=R_S(1+a),\qquad a=r_o\left(g_m-\frac1{R_S}\right)} .
\]

So you need \(g_mR_S>1\) to get positive voltage gain while keeping \(R_{in}=50\ \Omega\).

A first-order thermal-noise expression, neglecting gate-induced noise, correlation, flicker noise and capacitances, is

\[
F \approx 1+
\frac{\left(\gamma_1 g_{m1}+\gamma_2 g_{m2}\right)(a+2)^2}
{a^2 R_S\left(g_m+1/r_o\right)^2}
+
\frac{(1+a)\left(a+2r_o/R_S\right)^2}
{a^2\left(1+g_m r_o\right)^2 } .
\]

Design consequences:

- Use the PMOS/NMOS pair for current reuse: size them so the same DC current flows and the feedback-set DC point is near mid-supply. Roughly \(W_p/W_n\approx \mu_n/\mu_p\), adjusted for thresholds and \(\lambda\). This maximizes \(g_{m1}+g_{m2}\) for a given supply current.
- For a given current, move toward lower overdrive/larger \(W\) to raise \(g_m\) and intrinsic gain \(g_mr_o\), but stop when input capacitance, bandwidth, linearity, headroom or gate-induced noise degrade.
- After choosing \(g_m\) and \(r_o\), set \(R_F\) from the boxed equation. If \(r_o\) is large and gain is high, this reduces to the usual \(R_{in}\approx 1/g_m\), \(R_F\approx R_S(1+|A_v|)\), but use the exact equation when \(r_o\) is comparable to \(R_F\).
- Make \(C_1\) a short at the operating frequency: \(1/(\omega C_1)\ll 50\ \Omega\), with ESR much below \(50\ \Omega\). Remember

\[
C_{in}\approx C_{gs1}+C_{gs2}+(1+a)(C_{gd1}+C_{gd2}),
\]

so very large gain/width eventually breaks the broadband 50-Ω real input match. If narrowband, an input inductor would help, but that changes the shown topology.

In practice: sweep \(W/L\), bias current and \(R_F\) in the PDK noise simulation with the constraint \(\Re\{Z_{in}\}=50\ \Omega\) at the band of interest; the ideal thermal-noise equations push you toward higher \(g_m\), higher intrinsic gain and higher closed-loop gain, while the real optimum is set by parasitics, stability, power and linearity.

answers.question: Compute the input impedance of the circuit in the figure.

answer.text:
Assume \(V_{DD}\) and \(V_b\) are ac grounds, \(I_{SS}\) is ideal, the gate of \(M_1\) draws no current, and transistor capacitances other than \(C_{in}\) are neglected.

The first stage gives

\[
v_X=-g_{m1}R_{D1}v_P .
\]

The pair \(M_2/M_3\) steers the tail current, so the signal current delivered to the output node is

\[
i_o=\frac{g_{m2}g_{m3}}{g_{m2}+g_{m3}}v_X
\equiv -K v_P ,
\]

where

\[
K=g_{m1}R_{D1}\frac{g_{m2}g_{m3}}{g_{m2}+g_{m3}} .
\]

KCL at \(V_{out}\):

\[
-Kv_P=\frac{v_{out}}{R_{D2}}+\frac{v_{out}-v_P}{R_F}.
\]

Thus the feedback-path admittance at the input is

\[
\frac{v_P-v_{out}}{R_F}\frac1{v_P}
=
\frac{1+KR_{D2}}{R_F+R_{D2}} .
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
Z_{in}=
\left[
\frac1{R_{in}}+sC_{in}
+
\frac{1+KR_{D2}}{R_F+R_{D2}}
\right]^{-1}
}
\]

with \(K\) above. If \(M_2\) and \(M_3\) are matched, \(g_{m2}=g_{m3}=g_m\), so

\[
K=\frac12 g_{m1}g_m R_{D1}.
\]

For \(R_F\gg R_{D2}\), this reduces to the usual Miller result: the feedback resistor appears approximately as  
\(\displaystyle R_F/(1+KR_{D2})\) in parallel with \(R_{in}\) and \(1/(sC_{in})\). If keeping \(r_{o1}\), replace \(R_{D1}\) in \(K\) by \(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}\).

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The derived feedback admittance is exact and includes RD2: for matched M2/M3, A0 = K·RD2, so its inverse is (RF + RD2)/(1 + A0), as required. The additional Rin and Cin terms are shunt contributions and do not change that core result.

answers.question: Compute the input impedance of the circuit in the figure.

answer.text:
Assume small-signal operation and fixed bulk potentials. Let

\[
R_X=R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1},\qquad 
R_S=r_{o2}\quad(\text{ideal }I_{SS}),\qquad
R_O=R_{D2}\parallel r_{o3}.
\]

With \(R_F\) removed, the forward voltage gain from node \(P\) to \(V_{out}\) is

\[
A_{v0}=(-g_{m1}R_X)(-g_{m2}R_S)(-g_{m3}R_O)\equiv -G ,
\]

so

\[
G=g_{m1}(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1})\,g_{m2}r_{o2}\,
g_{m3}(R_{D2}\parallel r_{o3}) .
\]

Since the gate of \(M_1\) draws no current, the feedback resistor contributes an input admittance

\[
Y_F=\frac{1-A_{v0}}{R_F+R_O}
=\frac{1+G}{R_F+R_O}.
\]

Therefore the impedance seen by the input current source is

\[
\boxed{
Z_{in}(s)=
\left[
\frac{1}{R_{in}}+sC_{in}+
\frac{1+G}{R_F+R_O}
\right]^{-1}
}
\]

with \(G\) as above. For \(G\gg1\) and \(R_O\ll R_F\),

\[
Z_{in}(s)\approx
\left[
\frac{1}{R_{in}}+sC_{in}+\frac{G}{R_F}
\right]^{-1},
\]

i.e. the feedback resistor is referred to the input approximately as \(R_F/G\).

The added input resistance and capacitance are also not part of the requested result, so it misses the exact input impedance.

answers.question: If the LDO regulator in the figure generates thermal noise with spectrum Sth, how do we compute the VCO output phase noise?

answer.text:
Treat the LDO noise as a low-frequency modulation of the VCO supply, then map it to frequency/phase through the oscillator **supply-pushing gain**.

Let \(f_m\) be the offset from the carrier and use one-sided PSDs. First refer the LDO thermal noise to the VCO supply node:

\[
S_{V_s}(f_m)=|T_{\rm th\to V_{out}}(f_m)|^2 S_{\rm th}(f_m)
\]

If \(S_{\rm th}\) is already the LDO output-referred voltage-noise PSD, then \(T_{\rm th\to V_{out}}=1\).

Define

\[
K_s(f_m)=\frac{\partial f_{\rm osc}}{\partial V_{out}}
\quad [\text{Hz/V}] .
\]

The resulting frequency-noise PSD is

\[
S_{\delta f}(f_m)=|K_s(f_m)|^2 S_{V_s}(f_m),
\]

and since phase is the integral of frequency,

\[
S_\phi(f_m)=\frac{S_{\delta f}(f_m)}{f_m^2}.
\]

For small phase modulation, the single-sideband phase noise is

\[
\boxed{
\mathcal L(f_m)\simeq \frac{1}{2}S_\phi(f_m)
=
\frac{|K_s(f_m)|^2 S_{V_s}(f_m)}{2 f_m^2}
}
\]

in linear units, i.e. dBc/Hz \(=10\log_{10}\mathcal L(f_m)\). If your \(S_{\rm th}\) is a two-sided PSD, drop/adjust the factor \(1/2\) consistently.

For the tank shown, with matched sides and per-side capacitance  
\(C_s(V_{out},V_{cont})\), you may start from

\[
f_{\rm osc}\approx \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{L_1 C_s}}
\]

so that, to first order,

\[
K_s=
-\frac{f_{\rm osc}}{2C_s}
\frac{\partial C_s}{\partial V_{out}} .
\]

In practice, get \(K_s\) from a PSS/PNOISE simulation or by injecting a small sinusoid on \(V_{out}\): if a supply tone of rms amplitude \(v_{s,\rm rms}\) at \(f_m\) gives a measured sideband ratio \(\mathcal L_m\), then

\[
|K_s|=\frac{f_m\sqrt{2\mathcal L_m}}{v_{s,\rm rms}} .
\]

A flat LDO output voltage-noise spectrum therefore produces a VCO phase-noise term falling as \(1/f_m^2\). If the circuit were perfectly symmetric and the tail current source ideal, the direct common-mode supply-to-differential-phase coupling would be small; the residual effect comes from varactor/common-mode bias dependence, finite tail impedance, and device-imbalance AM/PM conversion.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly converts supply-pushing sensitivity into frequency noise and then phase noise with the expected 1/f_m^2 dependence. It does not explicitly state the key design implication that Kpush is closely related to KVCO and that reducing KVCO reduces this noise conversion; the symmetry caveat is also potentially confusing.

answers.question: If the LDO regulator in the figure generates thermal noise with spectrum Sth, how do we compute the VCO output phase noise?

answer.text:
Let \(f_m\) be the offset from the carrier and \(\omega_m=2\pi f_m\). Treat the LDO output noise as a voltage source \(v_n\) at \(V_{out}\) with one‑sided PSD \(S_{th}(f_m)\) [V\(^2\)/Hz] (if \(S_{th}\) is given in V/\(\sqrt{\text{Hz}}\), square it).

The computation has three steps.

**1. Supply noise that actually reaches the tank.**  
Include any transfer function from the LDO output to the tank common‑mode,
\[
V_{cm}(j\omega_m)=H_{sup}(j\omega_m)\,V_n(j\omega_m),
\]
set by the LDO output impedance, on‑chip decoupling, and the two \(L_1\)’s. For offsets \(f_m\ll f_0\) and no explicit supply filter, the inductors are short to the slow modulation, so \(H_{sup}\approx 1\) (the static drop \(I_{VCO}r_L/2\) does not modulate the frequency).

**2. Supply‑pushing gain.**  
Define
\[
K_\omega \equiv \frac{\partial \omega_0}{\partial V_{out}}
\quad [\text{rad/s/V}],
\qquad
\omega_0=\frac{1}{\sqrt{L_1 C_{eq}}}.
\]
Because \(L_1\) ties the DC level of \(X,Y\) to \(V_{out}\) while the varactors \(M_{v1},M_{v2}\) and banks \(B_{1,2}\) return to the quiet \(V_{cont}\)/ground, a change \(\delta V_{out}\) changes the varactor bias \(V_X-V_{cont}\). Thus
\[
K_\omega
=
-\frac{\omega_0}{2C_{eq}}\,
\frac{\partial C_{eq}}{\partial V_b}\,H_{sup}(0),
\qquad V_b=V_{X,dc}-V_{cont}.
\]
For the dominant varactor term, \(V_{out}\) and \(V_{cont}\) enter \(V_b\) with opposite signs, so this term has the **same magnitude as the corresponding VCO tuning gain**, \(K_{\omega,\text{push}}\approx -K_{VCO}\); the sign disappears in the noise PSD. Add supply‑referred nonlinear parasitics/AM–PM only if they are comparable.

**3. Convert frequency noise to phase noise.**
\[
S_f(f_m)=\left(\frac{K_\omega}{2\pi}\right)^2 |H_{sup}(f_m)|^2 S_{th}(f_m),
\]
\[
S_\phi(f_m)=\frac{S_f(f_m)}{f_m^2}
=\left(\frac{K_\omega}{\omega_m}\right)^2 |H_{sup}(f_m)|^2 S_{th}(f_m).
\]

Hence the single‑sideband phase noise is
\[
\boxed{\;
\mathcal L(f_m)=\tfrac12 S_\phi(f_m)
=
\tfrac12\left(\frac{K_\omega\,|H_{sup}(f_m)|}{\omega_m}\right)^{\!2} S_{th}(f_m)
\;}
\]
or in dBc/Hz, \(10\log_{10}\mathcal L(f_m)\).

For white LDO thermal noise (\(S_{th}\) flat) and constant \(K_\omega\), this contribution falls as \(1/f_m^2\), i.e. \(-20\) dB/dec; any \(1/f\) part of the LDO noise becomes \(1/f_m^3\) at the VCO output. Equivalently, in the Hajimiri–Lee picture this is the low‑frequency (DC) value of the supply‑node sensitivity function.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies supply pushing, converts LDO voltage noise through the VCO’s frequency sensitivity and FM-to-phase relation with the 1/f_m² dependence, and notes the direct varactor coupling makes the pushing gain closely related to K_VCO. The extra transfer-function details and factor conventions do not undermine the result.

answers.question: If the LDO regulator in the figure generates thermal noise with spectrum Sth, how do we compute the VCO output phase noise?

answer.text:
Treat the LDO noise as a small common-mode modulation of the VCO supply node \(V_{\text{out}}\). The relevant gain is the **supply-pushing gain**, not the normal tuning gain from \(V_{\text{cont}}\).

Let the LDO output voltage-noise PSD referred to the VCO supply node be

\[
S_v(f)=S_{\text{th}}(f)
\]

if \(S_{\text{th}}\) is already the noise at \(V_{\text{out}}\); otherwise first refer it through the LDO output impedance/decoupling network. Define

\[
K_{\text{push}}(f)=\frac{\partial f_0}{\partial V_{\text{out}}}
\qquad [\text{Hz/V}]
\]

and let \(H_{cm}(f)\) be the small-signal transfer from the LDO noise source to the common-mode voltage at nodes \(X/Y\). For low offset frequencies \(H_{cm}\approx 1\); near/above the common-mode resonance formed by the two \(L_1\)’s and node/tail capacitances, compute it explicitly.

Then the supply noise becomes frequency noise

\[
S_{\Delta f}(f)=
\left|K_{\text{push}}(f)H_{cm}(f)\right|^2 S_v(f),
\]

and phase noise is

\[
S_\phi(f)=\frac{S_{\Delta f}(f)}{f^2},
\qquad
\boxed{
\mathcal L(f)=
\frac{S_\phi(f)}{2}
=
\frac{
\left|K_{\text{push}}(f)H_{cm}(f)\right|^2 S_v(f)
}{
2f^2
}
}
\]

with \(\mathcal L(f)\) in linear SSB phase noise; use \(10\log_{10}\) for dBc/Hz. Equivalently, in angular-frequency form replace \(K_{\text{push}}/f\) by \(K_\omega/\omega_m\), where \(K_\omega=\partial\omega_0/\partial V_{\text{out}}\).

A first-order estimate for the pushing gain is

\[
K_{\text{push}}
\approx
-\frac{f_0}{2C_{\text{eff}}}
\frac{\partial C_{\text{eff}}}{\partial V_{\text{out}}},
\]

where \(C_{\text{eff}}\) is the effective large-signal capacitance of each half-circuit. For a nonlinear node capacitance,

\[
C_{\text{eff}}
=
\frac{1}{\pi}
\int_0^{2\pi}
C_{\text{node}}\!\left(
V_{\text{out}}-V_{\text{cont}}+A\cos\theta
\right)
\sin^2\theta \, d\theta ,
\]

plus an amplitude term
\((\partial C_{\text{eff}}/\partial A)(\partial A/\partial V_{\text{out}})\) if the swing changes with supply.

Important caveat: in a perfectly balanced oscillator with linear capacitors and an ideal tail current source, LDO noise is common-mode and gives ideally zero phase noise. The finite contribution comes mainly from MOS varactors/junction capacitances biased by \(V_{\text{out}}-V_{\text{cont}}\), finite tail-source impedance, device mismatch, and AM-to-PM conversion. In simulation, use PSS/PXF or measure \(K_{\text{push}}\) by perturbing \(V_{\text{out}}\); do not use the \(V_{\text{cont}}\) tuning gain. White LDO noise gives a \(1/f^2\) phase-noise contribution; LDO flicker noise gives a \(1/f^3\) contribution, assuming \(K_{\text{push}}\) is constant.

It does not clearly state the key design implication that Kpush is closely related to KVCO and that reducing KVCO reduces this noise conversion; the common-mode cancellation caveat also risks obscuring the direct varactor-coupling mechanism in this circuit.

answers.question: We add CT to the tail node, as in the figure. What happens to the phase noise?

answer.text:
It goes down (the tail contribution to phase noise is suppressed).

Why: at the oscillation frequency the sources of \(M_1/M_2\) (node \(P\)) are a differential virtual ground — the sum \(i_{M1}+i_{M2}\) contains only DC and even harmonics (\(2f_0,4f_0,\dots\)), no \(f_0\) term. So \(C_T\) ideally carries no fundamental current and does **not** load the tank or reduce its \(Q\)/amplitude.

What \(C_T\) does is short node \(P\) to ground at \(2f_0\). That helps two ways:

- The strong \(2f_0\) common‑mode ripple at \(P\) now flows through \(C_T\) instead of modulating \(V_{GS}\)/\(V_{DS}\) of \(M_1,M_2\). The pair is less pushed toward triode and its effective ISF to tail‑node noise is reduced (less AM/AM‑PM and less cyclostationary noise conversion).
- The tail current source’s broadband noise near \(2f_0\), which the switching pair would otherwise mix down to \(f_0\) (\(2f_0-f_0\)) through \(i_{\text{diff}}\approx I_{SS}\,\mathrm{sgn}(v_{XY})\), is largely bypassed through \(C_T\) to ground rather than being commutated into the tank.

For a large \(C_T\) the pair is also driven toward a more pulsed, class‑C‑like conduction (devices off near the zero crossings, current delivered near the peaks where the ISF is small), which further improves the phase‑noise/current efficiency up to an optimum.

Caveats: \(C_T\) is open at low frequency, so it does **not** remove up‑conversion of the tail device’s \(1/f\) noise — the close‑in \(1/f^3\) corner is essentially unchanged unless the tail device is made large/low‑flicker. With mismatch, \(P\) can move slightly at \(f_0\), so a very large \(C_T\) may marginally detune/load the tank; otherwise it is benign for start‑up (differential loop gain is unchanged).

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It mentions an optimum and class-C-like conduction, but mainly argues that filtering makes phase noise decrease. It misses the key class-C mechanism of peak tank currents exceeding ISS and the Razavi degradations (flicker-noise upconversion, triode operation, or low-frequency instability), so the claimed optimum is only generic.

answers.question: We add CT to the tail node, as in the figure. What happens to the phase noise?

answer.text:
It should **reduce the phase-noise contribution from the tail branch**—if \(C_T\) is a clean RF bypass.

For the differential signal, node \(P\) is ideally a common-mode/virtual node, so \(C_T\) does not set the main oscillation frequency. But the switching pair and \(I_{SS}\) generate common-mode/second-harmonic currents at \(P\). The capacitor stiffens \(v_P\) and gives those RF/\(2f_0\) currents a low-impedance path to ground, so less tail-current noise is commutated into the tank.

With a large \(C_T\), the core also moves toward **class-C** operation: for the same average \(I_{SS}\), current is delivered in shorter pulses near the tank-voltage peaks, where phase sensitivity is low. Ideally the fundamental current can increase from \(\sim \frac{4}{\pi}I_{SS}\) toward \(2I_{SS}\), giving up to

\[
20\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\approx 3.9\text{ dB}
\]

phase-noise improvement in a current-limited oscillator.

Caveats: \(C_T\) does **not** remove low-frequency flicker noise of the tail current source, and a lossy/mistuned tail capacitance can create a common-mode resonance/squegging or extra AM–PM conversion, which would degrade phase noise.

answers.question: We add CT to the tail node, as in the figure. What happens to the phase noise?

answer.text:
It gets **worse** (the close‑in phase noise rises). The “just bypass the tail” intuition backfires for this topology.

Why:

- For the *differential* signal, node P is still a virtual ground, so \(C_T\) does not move \(\omega_0\) or the swing to first order. Its effect is on the common mode / even harmonics and on noise folding.
- Node P is *supposed* to bounce: each source follows the higher gate, so P naturally carries a large \(|\cos\omega_0 t|\) (strong \(2\omega_0\)) component. With a high‑impedance tail, the ON transistor keeps a roughly constant, moderate \(V_{GS}\) and stays in (reverse) saturation — high output resistance, light loading of the tank.
- Shorting P to ground with \(C_T\) clamps that bounce. Then, at each peak, the ON device has its gate high while its drain sits at the opposite (low) node, so \(V_{GS}\) is pumped up by the swing \(A\) while \(V_{DS}\) collapses: M1/M2 are driven deep into triode once per half‑cycle. In triode they present a small resistance across the tank (lower effective \(Q\)) and inject more channel noise. By Leeson/Hajimiri, \(\mathcal{L}\{\Delta\omega\}\propto F/Q^{2}\,(\omega_0/\Delta\omega)^2/P_{sig}\), so \(Q_{eff}\downarrow\) and \(F\uparrow\) → phase noise up.

- In addition, for common‑mode signals \(L_1\) and \(L_2\) are in parallel to the AC‑grounded \(V_{DD}\), i.e. \(L_{cm}=L/2\), and they resonate with \(C_T\) at  
  \[
  \omega_{cm}\approx \frac{1}{\sqrt{(L/2)\,C_T}} .
  \]
  The commutating pair pumps common‑mode current into P at \(2\omega_0\); if \(\omega_{cm}\) approaches \(2\omega_0\) (note \(C_T\approx C_{\text{tank}}\) gives \(\omega_{cm}\approx2\omega_0\)), the tail node develops a large second‑harmonic voltage that folds tail/device noise and AM→PM into the carrier — phase noise degrades sharply, with possible spurious/common‑mode oscillation or start‑up trouble.

Caveats: \(C_T\) is open at DC, so it does **not** remove up‑converted tail‑source \(1/f\) noise; the only potentially helpful action is shunting a *real* tail source’s RF/\(2\omega_0\) thermal noise. The correct way to get that benefit without clamping P is to keep P **high‑impedance at \(2\omega_0\)** — an inductor in series with the tail current source, with the bypass capacitor placed on the current‑source side (Hegazi–Sjöland–Abidi filter) — rather than tying a capacitor from P to ground. (If \(I_{SS}\) were an ideal noiseless source, \(C_T\) would change none of the ideal currents, but with real devices the triode‑loading/common‑mode‑resonance penalty dominates.)

It misses the class-C-like regime in which peak tank currents exceed ISS and can improve phase noise, so it does not capture the nonmonotonic effect.

\[
\boxed{f_{\rm osc}\approx \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{L_{\rm eq}C_{\rm eq}}}
= \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{L C_X}} } .
\]

If capacitance is truly neglected, the ideal schematic has no finite oscillation frequency; a real circuit oscillates through parasitic capacitance.

For strongly quadrature-coupled cores, include a small pulling term:

\[
f_{\rm osc}\approx f_0\left[1\pm \frac{1}{2Q}\frac{g_{m,c}}{g_m}\right]
\approx f_0\left[1\pm \frac{1}{2Q}\frac{I_1}{I_{SS}}\right],
\]

with the sign set by the quadrature phase sequence. A numerical value requires \(L\), \(C_X\) and, for the correction, tank \(Q\).
